At 2026-04-09T13:22:10Z the primary node redis-cache-2 was marked down after 3 consecutive PING timeouts, and at 13:22:52Z replica redis-cache-3 was promoted to primary with an EMPTY dataset ('replica was resyncing'). market-data-service then logged 23 'cache miss storm: quote:<id> not in redis-cache' WARNs from 13:22:25Z, rebuilding from the exchange feed (1034-8748ms). So H1 is positively supported by a real failover/empty-dataset event, not by a metric reset. Note the cache exposes no uptime/restart/last_save/rdb_last_bgsave/keyspace counters (only connected_clients, cpu_pct, evictions_per_min, hit_ratio_pct, memory_pct) - a permanent data gap, so the restart corroboration rests on logs alone.

portfolio-service's error_rate did NOT move at the onset: it stayed flat at 0.13-0.31% (mean 0.21) across 13:10-13:30Z, with 13:20Z avg 0.18 and 13:22Z avg 0.19. The shared-cache consumer's degradation is therefore latency-only, unlike the quote-path services which also raised 5xx error_rate.

critiques.summary: H1 is adequately proven and no further obtainable evidence remains. The causal chain is grounded in directly observed evidence at every load-bearing hop: (1) redis-cache is a verified shared cache of both pricing-engine and market-data-service (F1/F15/F17); (2) its hit_ratio collapsed 96%->12.86% and memory 70%->7.25% at 13:18-13:24Z while evictions and CPU stayed flat (F25-F28), the signature of an emptied cache; (3) the emptying is explained by a REAL failover, not a metric reset — explicit logs show redis-cache-2 marked down 13:22:10Z and empty, still-resyncing replica redis-cache-3 promoted 13:22:52Z, with no RDB reload (F38/F40); (4) market-data-service then logged a matching cache-miss storm from 13:22:25Z, i.e. its miss-rebuilds BEGIN ~15s AFTER the primary-down marking, establishing sub-bucket temporal order and sandwiching the service slowdown inside the cache failure (F41); (5) market-data-service CPU rose only AFTER latency (F31/F35), so its CPU load is consequence, not cause; (6) scope is explained completely — pricing-engine (F7-F9), market-data-service (F10), api-gateway as pass-through (F11/F46), AND the decisive discriminator, the non-quote-path cache consumer portfolio-service stepping in lockstep (F43/F48), while non-cache controls stayed flat (F45). Alternatives are affirmatively contradicted: H2 by F31/F35/F32 (CPU-after-latency, flat request_rate/memory) despite a single flagged ASSUMED hop in its chain; H5 by flat exchange-gateway p99/error/upstream_latency at onset (F34/F36); H3 closed by per-service deploy/config scans counting 0 with partial:false (F19/F20/F21); H4 rejected on scope (F14), timing (F7), mechanism (F9), and control data (F45). The confidence cap of 0.85 (below the stated 0.78-driven over-claim risk) reflects two honest residuals: redis-cache's own latency/uptime/keyspace counters and the vendor feed are PERMANENT data gaps (F37/F42/F47/F23), and portfolio-service's direct redis-cache edge was inferred from its role and timing rather than fetched — but neither touches the load-bearing mechanism, which is positively observed via the failover log and the two-sided miss storm.

challenges.issue: The cache's own response-time contribution is unmeasured: redis-cache exposes no latency_p99_ms series, no uptime/restart/last_save/keyspace counters (F37/F42/F47), so the mechanism rests on the failover log plus two-sided miss-storm logs and the hit-ratio/memory collapse rather than a measured cache latency. This is a permanent data gap, not evidence against H1.

portfolio-service's direct binding to redis-cache was inferred from its role as a market-data-service upstream caller (F17) plus timing, not fetched from the dependency graph; if it were NOT a redis-cache consumer, the strongest shared-vs-local discriminator weakens. However the failover log + market-data miss storm independently establish the shared-cache mechanism.

Sub-300s ordering between the hit-ratio transition (13:18Z bucket) and the quote-path p99 step (13:20Z bucket) is not resolvable from metrics alone; the causal precedence is carried by the 13:22:10Z primary-down vs 13:22:25Z first-miss log timing and by F31/F35 (CPU-after-latency).

H2's literal 'resources at ceiling at onset' form is not just unsupported but actively contradicted: market-data-service CPU was flat ~44-47% at the 13:20-13:21Z latency onset and only rose to 86-94% at 13:22Z (F31/F35), with request_rate and memory flat (F32) — the opposite of a resource ceiling causing the slowdown.
